title: What child safety training do Victoria's Child Safe Standards require?
description: What Child Safe Standard 8 requires for staff and volunteer training in Victoria, how the Social Services Regulator assesses it, and how to evidence it.
shortAnswer: Victoria's Child Safe Standard 8 requires organizations covered by the Child Wellbeing and Safety Act 2005 (Vic) to equip staff and volunteers with the knowledge, skills and awareness to keep children safe through ongoing education and training. Minimum requirement 8.1 is training and support to implement the organization's Child Safety and Wellbeing Policy. Requirements 8.2 to 8.4 add recognizing harm, responding to concerns, and building culturally safe environments.
keyTakeaways: Victoria's 11 Child Safe Standards are mandatory under the Child Wellbeing and Safety Act 2005 (Vic) for organizations that provide services or facilities specifically for children or engage a child as an employee, contractor or volunteer. The current Standards took effect on July 1, 2022.

Standard 8 has four minimum requirements: training and support to implement the Child Safety and Wellbeing Policy (8.1), recognizing indicators of harm including harm caused by other children (8.2), responding to concerns and supporting colleagues who disclose harm (8.3), and building culturally safe environments (8.4).

The regulator's compliance indicators expect a training action plan, a training register, policy training at induction and at regular intervals, and leaders telling staff and volunteers that child safety training is mandatory.
Responsibility for the Standards transferred from the Commission for Children and Young People to the Social Services Regulator (SSR) in February 2026. The SSR is one of five co-regulators.
Failure to comply with an SSR improvement notice carries a maximum civil penalty of 1,200 penalty units for a body corporate, which the SSR states is more than $250,900 in 2026 to 27.
regulator: Social Services Regulator (SSR), with four sector co-regulators: the Victorian Registration and Qualifications Authority, the Victorian Early Childhood Regulatory Authority, the Department of Health, and Workforce Inspectorate Victoria
appliesTo: Organizations in Victoria that provide services or facilities specifically for children, including where only some programs are for children
Organizations that engage a child as an employee, contractor or volunteer

Sectors listed in Schedule 1 of the Child Wellbeing and Safety Act 2005 (Vic), such as schools, early childhood services, hospitals, sport and recreation, religious bodies, charities, disability and housing services, and local and state government bodies
All staff and volunteers in those organizations, and the leaders responsible for child safety

sections.heading: What does Child Safe Standard 8 require?

blocks.text: Standard 8 requires that "Staff and volunteers are equipped with the knowledge, skills and awareness to keep children and young people safe through ongoing education and training." Each Standard is an expected outcome, and the regulator's [Complying with the Child Safe Standards](https://www.vic.gov.au/complying-child-safe-standards) page sets out four minimum requirements that an organization must, at a minimum, ensure for Standard 8.

blocks.caption: Child Safe Standard 8: minimum requirements (text as published by the SSR)
head: Requirement
Text
rows: Staff and volunteers are trained and supported to effectively implement the organisation's Child Safety and Wellbeing Policy.
Staff and volunteers receive training and information to recognise indicators of child harm including harm caused by other children and young people.
Staff and volunteers receive training and information to respond effectively to issues of child safety and wellbeing and support colleagues who disclose harm.
Staff and volunteers receive training and information on how to build culturally safe environments for children and young people.

blocks.text: Requirement 8.1 depends on the Child Safety and Wellbeing Policy that the organization must have under the governance Standard, so training cannot be finalized until that policy exists. The regulator describes induction, ongoing training and professional development, and supervision and management as the three ways to meet Standard 8.

An organization in Victoria usually must comply if it provides services or facilities specifically for children, or engages a child as a contractor, employee or volunteer, and falls within a category in Schedule 1 of the [Child Wellbeing and Safety Act 2005 (Vic)](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/child-wellbeing-and-safety-act-2005). A child is anyone under 18.

"Specifically for children" does not mean only for children. The SSR's [guidance on who must comply](https://www.vic.gov.au/who-child-safe-standards-apply) gives the example of a gym that serves adults but also runs gymnastics classes for children, which must comply. Organizations covered by the Reportable Conduct Scheme must also comply with the Standards.

For organizations that must comply, the [SSR states](https://www.vic.gov.au/introduction-child-safe-standards) that the Standards are law and are mandatory within Victoria, and that organizations must comply with all aspects of the Standards at all times. All 11 Standards must be implemented, not only the training Standard.

sections.heading: Who regulates the Child Safe Standards in Victoria?

blocks.text: Five co-regulators share the work, and the Social Services Regulator (SSR) took over the Commission for Children and Young People's role in February 2026. The SSR's [guide for creating a child safe organization](https://www.vic.gov.au/guide-creating-child-safe-organisation) (version 6, October 2026) records that the Child Safe Standards and the Reportable Conduct Scheme transferred to the SSR in February 2026 as part of reforms responding to the Victorian Rapid Child Safety Review.

blocks.text: The SSR guide notes that where a co-regulator has issued different guidance for its sector, organizations in that sector should follow the co-regulator's guidance. Policies, training content and induction packs written before February 2026 often name the Commission as regulator and should be updated.

sections.heading: What evidence does the regulator look for?

blocks.text: The SSR assesses Standard 8 against published compliance indicators, and states that organizations will generally comply if they produce these documents and take these actions in a way that achieves the Standard. An organization that does something different may need to explain how its approach meets the outcome and minimum requirements.

items: **Training action plan** covering the Child Safety and Wellbeing Policy, indicators of abuse and harm, supporting a person making a disclosure, responding to concerns including internal and external reporting, notifying families and carers and managing risks, and supporting cultural safety.
**Guidance materials** such as policies, procedures, information sheets and posters on the same topics.
**A training register** that records completion of training by staff and volunteers.
**Leadership communication** that child safety training is mandatory.
**Policy training at induction and at regular intervals.**
**Training that is fit for purpose:** appropriate to the organization's engagement with children, trauma-informed, offered regularly so knowledge stays current, and regularly reviewed and updated.
**Supervision and management** that includes identifying child safety training needs.

blocks.text: The October 2026 guide adds practical expectations. Induction should happen before any work with children begins and should also be given to people who change roles. It should equip staff and volunteers to implement the policy, understand the Code of Conduct, identify and respond to harm including disclosures, meet reporting obligations, provide culturally safe environments, and follow record keeping and information sharing obligations. The guide also suggests content warnings and support options because training on harm can be confronting for survivors.

sections.heading: How does Standard 8 map to learning outcomes and evidence?

blocks.text: Each minimum requirement can be written as a learning outcome with an assessment point and a record the regulator can inspect. The mapping below is original and illustrative, not an SSR template; it follows [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations).

blocks.text: A [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) that lists every staff and volunteer role against these modules, with refresh dates, makes the "regular intervals" indicator auditable. The regulator does not set a frequency; [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) covers how to choose and justify one.

sections.heading: What happens if an organization does not comply?

blocks.text: The SSR takes a risk based and graduated approach, and can escalate from education and advice to improvement notices, enforceable undertakings and court action. Its powers come from the Child Wellbeing and Safety Act 2005 (Vic) and the Social Services Regulation Act 2021 (Vic), as described on the SSR's page on [how the Standards are regulated](https://www.vic.gov.au/how-child-safe-standards-are-regulated).

items: **Improvement notice:** sets out the non-compliance, the action required and a timeframe. Failure to comply carries a maximum civil penalty of 1,200 penalty units for a body corporate (more than $250,900 in 2026 to 27) and 240 penalty units for an individual (more than $50,100).

**Notice to produce:** failing to comply is subject to a maximum penalty of 300 penalty units for a body corporate (more than $62,700) and 60 penalty units for an individual (more than $12,500). The same maximums apply to obstructing an authorized officer and to giving false or misleading information.
**Enforceable undertakings,** recorded on a public register, and court orders, declarations, injunctions and adverse publicity orders.

blocks.text: A training register is often the first document requested, so gaps in records turn a practice issue into an evidence issue. See [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each Standard 8 minimum requirement and compliance indicator as an obligation linked to the organization's Child Safety and Wellbeing Policy, Code of Conduct and reporting procedures, and defines role based learning outcomes and assessment points for staff, volunteers and leaders. When the policy or the regulator's guidance changes, the linked modules and assessments can be found and reviewed.

faqs.q: Do volunteers need child safety training under the Victorian Standards?
faqs.a: Yes. Every Standard 8 minimum requirement names staff and volunteers. The compliance indicators expect the training register to record completion by volunteers as well as staff, and the SSR guide says induction should take place before any work with children begins, including for volunteers.

faqs.q: How often must child safety training be refreshed in Victoria?
faqs.a: The Standards do not set a fixed frequency. The compliance indicators expect policy training at induction and at regular intervals, and training offered on a regular basis so knowledge and skills stay current. Organizations should set and document a refresh cycle that suits their engagement with children and record it in the training register.

faqs.q: Does the Commission for Children and Young People still regulate the Standards?
faqs.a: No. The Social Services Regulator states that responsibility transferred to it from the Commission for Children and Young People in February 2026. The SSR now publishes the guidance and compliance indicators, and four sector co-regulators continue to regulate schools, early childhood services, health services and licensed child employers.

faqs.q: How do the Victorian Standards relate to the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations?
faqs.a: The SSR guide explains that a 2019 Victorian review recommended changes to align the Child Safe Standards more closely with the National Principles, and the updated 11 Standards took effect on July 1, 2022. Organizations operating nationally still need to meet the Victorian minimum requirements and compliance indicators in Victoria.
